messages.subject: Re: RSFs
messages.subject_clean: RSFs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,

That shouldn't be an issue. The uncertainties are propagated informed by the autocorrelation (or lack thereof). But you would want to calculate new UDs from the kill sites and bed sites, and not use the track UDs for that. The important information in the UDs that is leveraged by rsf.fit() are the weights, movement model, and DOF, which need to correspond to the data.

Best,
Chris

On Wednesday, August 30, 2023 at 4:47:58 AM UTC-4 lukedaniel...@googlemail.com wrote:
> Hi Chris,
>
> Thanks for the reply! :)
>
> Re. my previous question:
> 3. Previously you said: "The dataset that goes into rsf.fit() needs to be the same as what went into the akde() weights, or the weights and data points will not match."
>
> I want to create RSFs to assess habitat selection for kill sites and bed sites for each puma (for which we have these data) and determine if habitat attributes associated with kills sites and bed sites differ from each other, and if they also differ from general habitat use use across the entire home range (based on all locations from movement data). I also want to look at potential differences between seasonal habitat selection, hence I was planning on building the following 9 RSFs per individual and then calculating mean() parameter coefficients from each (not all individuals have kill site and bed site data though, so the number of individuals contributing to each mean() population level parameter coefficient will vary).
>
> RSFs per individual:
> 1. all locations
> 2. all kill sites
> 3. all bed sites
> 4. winter only locations
> 5. winter only kill sites
> 6. winter only bed sites
> 7. summer locations
> 8. summer kill sites
> 9. summer bed sites
>
> Creating RSFs for 1, 4 & 9 above seems to be fine because the number of locations/weights informing the UD created by akde() will remain the same for rsf.select()/rsf.fit(), because I will split the data based on season and create seasonal UDs and run seasonal RSFs accordingly.
>
> In previous correspondence with Jesse, I had asked:
>
> "Is rsf.fit appropriate for fitting RSFs to bed and kill sites for individual pumas when we might only have 5-40 bed or kill sites per individual?"
>
> and he said
>
> "Yes. The movement model selected will likely be IID, but that's fine--just means adjusting for autocorrelation isn't important"
>
> However, given kill sites and bed sites represent a very limited number of locations per individual, and this number obviously doesn't represent the same number of locations/weights informing the UD/home range for each individual, it appears I can't use rsf.select()/rsf.fit() to create RSFs for kill and bed sites per puma because the accompanying UD will be based on hundreds or thousands of locations and the kill or bed site locations represent only a handful of these, e.g. 10 - 30 locations in some cases.
>
> Does this mean that there is no way of running the kill and bed site part of my analysis in ctmm, and instead I would need to use a more traditional RSF approach of sampling a random number of available but "unused" locations per kill or bed site location within an individual's home range to determine habitat selection and parameter coefficients associated with kill and bed sites? Or is there a way of using an individual's UD in rsf.select()/rsf.fit() but suppressing the need for the number of weights to match the number of locations (i.e. kill sites or bed sites), for which we want to determine parameter coefficients?
>
> Hope that makes sense now.
>
> Cheers,
> Luke
>
>
> On Wednesday, 30 August 2023 at 00:12:03 UTC+10 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hi Luke,
> >
> > 1.a) You want to include selected models to avoid ill-conditioned covariance matrices, but that selection needn't be strong. You don't need to test for significance.
> >
> > mean() allows for missing predictors. You just need to structure the interactions consistently. For instance:
> >
> > ~ tree_cover + tree_cover:day
> >
> > could equivalently be modeled as
> >
> > ~tree_cover + tree_cover:night
> >
> > or
> >
> > ~tree_cover:day + tree_cover:night
> >
> > but you want a consistent choice here that also makes sense for model selection to first be able to select the largest overall effect and then be able to refine that with additional terms.
> >
> > 1.b) Looks fine to me.
> > 2.) With the null model, NA predictor values aren't ensured to work when the predictors aren't being used, whereas offset()will be maintained going forward.
> > 3.) I'm not sure what you are asking here. How do you plan to make this comparison?
> >
> > Best,
> > Chris

> > >
> > > 1. "You would want to structure the models so that you are selecting among a null model, a model with an overall main effect, and a model with an overall main effect + an interaction that is on-average zero and provides extra detail to the main-effect model. If you don't or can't structure the models so that the interpretations are the same as you add predictors, then you could very well end up averaging coefficients nonsensically."
> > >
> > > I was originally thinking I could just throw all my predictor rasters into rsf.select(), extract the best performing model for each individual puma based on AICc, then calculate population level mean parameter coefficients for each parameter that appears in the best performing model per puma by using mean() function. However, based on what you said it might not be this simple.
> > >
> > > a) Based on your comment above, when determining whether it is appropriate to calculate the mean() of parameter coefficients across best fit models for each puma, would below be a suitable workflow?
> > >      i) Run rsf.select()/rsf.fit() on all predictors and review AICc of all models using verbose = TRUE
> > >      ii) Review the model outputs and ensure that the best fit model has significantly more support than the NULL model (i.e. NULL model is >2 delta AICc) (Or does this not matter if calculating mean() parameter coefficients across the population? Would I just include the best fit model in the mean() calculations even if the NULL is <2 delta AICc?)
> > >      iii) Ensure that coefficients for the main effects/predictors/parameters of the best fit model remain consistent/similar across all other models (Or just models that are <2 delta AICc?)
> > >      iii) If the best fit model doesn't contain any interaction terms, then ensure that the confidence interval for the interaction term coefficient crosses zero in other models (e.g. ~tree_cover+ tree_cover:distance_to_road    -   $CI  tree_cover:distance_to_road   low =  -2.1734673    est = 0.4598783    high = 3.093224). (Or should this just be done for models <2 delta AICc that contain interaction terms composed of the main effects from the best fit model?)
> > >      iv) If the best fit model contains main effects and interaction term/s then ensure the coefficients of main effects remain consistent/similar across other models (all models?)
> > >      v) If the best fit model contains only an interaction term, then review other models <2 delta AICc and if there is a model containing the main effects and interaction terms of the best fit model and the main effects do not cross zero, then select model with main effects and interaction term (e.g. ~ A + B + A:B  or  ~ A + A:B  or  ~B + A:B) (Would this be appropriate?)
> > >      vi) If these conditions are met then use the model as part of mean() parameter estimate calculations, if not, remove the model
> > >
> > > b) If for example I want to assess the selection of ~aspect + tree_cover + distance_to_water + distance_to_road + terrain_roughness + tree_cover:distance_to_road, using rsf.select(), and the best fit RSF models for multiple pumas were per below, and the parameter/model selection meet the criteria outlined above, is it appropriate to then calculate the population mean() parameter coefficients across all the non NULL models?
> > > Puma 1 = ~ tree_cover + terrain_roughness
> > > Puma 2 =  ~ tree_cover + distance_to_road
> > > Puma 3 = ~ distance_to_water + tree_cover:distance_to_road
> > > Puma 4 = ~ tree_cover + tree_cover:distance_to_road
> > > Puma 5 = ~  tree_cover:distance_to_road
> > > Puma 6 = ~ distance_to_road
> > > Puma 7 = ~ tree_cover
> > > Puma 8 = NULL model
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > 2. "For the moment, you need to remove those points at the beginning of the analysis, but I'm going to try to have an argument for that in rsf.fit() within a couple of weeks. But removing those data points is not the same as making that area unavailable in the RSF model."
> > >
> > > Apologies if I wasn't clear in my previous question. I have removed puma locations that fall within water before calculating UDs through akde(), and I have made areas of water "no data" in the predictor rasters, and these areas of water are represented by value of 0 in the offset_raster. Given this, I assume the use of an offset_raster in the rsf.select() formula will be redundant because I have already made the areas of water "no data" in the predictor rasters (i.e. 0 values in offset_raster). Is this correct or am I misinterpreting what offset() does?
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > 3. Previously you said: "The dataset that goes into rsf.fit() needs to be the same as what went into the akde() weights, or the weights and data points will not match."
> > >
> > > I was hoping to use rsf.select()/rsf.fit() to also assess habitat selection of puma kill sites and bed sites relative to available habitat across their entire home range (i.e. their UD), but we typically only have 10 to 30 kill or bed site locations per puma. Is this going to be a problem when the UD dataset is based on hundreds or thousands of locations (and weights), and the kill or bed site location data only contains 10 to 30 locations (i.e. the UD and kill or bed site datasets don't match)? > > >

> > > Luke

> > > > You would want to structure the models so that you are selecting among a null model, a model with an overall main effect, and a model with an overall main effect + an interaction that is on-average zero and provides extra detail to the main-effect model. If you don't or can't structure the models so that the interpretations are the same as you add predictors, then you could very well end up averaging coefficients nonsensically.
> > > > Yes, but I would recommend a simple rescaling of the predictors so that you never worry about back transforming.
> > > > For the moment, you need to remove those points at the beginning of the analysis, but I'm going to try to have an argument for that in rsf.fit() within a couple of weeks. But removing those data points is not the same as making that area unavailable in the RSF model.

messages.body_plain:
Hi!
I'm trying to extract the level.UD = 0.25 of a large UD, as a result of following your script for averaging UDS (presented in a spring webinar). It worked on a subset of my data (yay!), but for another dataset, I got the error message when trying to convert it to a SpatialPolygonsDataFrame: Error in CL[[row]] : subscript out of bounds. I noticed that if I extract anything below level 0.34, I get the error so that is the threshold. Is it possible to correct this error and extract the 25% contour for a shapefile? If not, what is the best way to understand what the bounds are for a UD object?

When I plotted the UD object, the plot did show the 25% contour.
# sample code to plot, taken from the webinar but inputting my own data:
UDS <- akde(data, FIT1)
MEAN.UD <- mean(UDS)
plot(data, MEAN.UD, level = 0.95, level.UD = 0.25) #see attached of plot

# code for extracting 0.25 level
# this worked:
UD_34 <- SpatialPolygonsDataFrame.UD(MEAN.UD, convex = FALSE, level.UD = 0.34, level = 0.95)
# this threw an error:
UD_25 <- SpatialPolygonsDataFrame.UD(MEAN.UD, convex = FALSE, level.UD = 0.25, level = 0.95)

Thank you for any insights!
Connie

messages.body_plain:
Hello Chris,

I came back to this issue after a couple of months. I want to incorporate the change in NDVI over time, so I wrote a code called find_ndvi(coordinate, time) to return the NDVI value of a location at a certain time. I was wondering if either of the methods below could work for my data set:

1. Extracting the coordinate, timestamp, and weight of each available point and conduct a weighed logistic regression (simple GLM)
- You mentioned that it is possible to plot the points generated by the Gaussian availability model in the previous discussion <https://groups.google.com/g/ctmm-user/c/v2yeJGalKiI/m/tS4i0HblAQAJ>. Therefore, I was wondering if we can plot the available points, can we extract the coordinates, timestamp, weights, and effective sample size (N) for each point using ctmm package and how (I am thinking about using Riemann integration)?

2. Modifying the code of rsf.select to incorporate find_ndvi function for NDVI value extraction
- I tried to figure out how formula works, but I am not sure if "formula" can be used as a place to put a function command (in my understanding, formula is an object to specify the relationship of elements in R=list() that I want to test? not sure if this is correct). I was wondering if there is any way that I can modify the code to extract time-dependent values for my data points.

I am sorry for bothering you multiple times with the same issue. Any thoughts and information would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you so much for your time.

Best regards,

Fang

Hi Fang,

You would need to sample a set of available points for each time, like you do in SSFs, because the normalization is different for every time.
Riemann integration would be slow in the time dependent case, because of having on integral per time.
Until I finish the time-dependent code in rsf.fit(), finding some time-dependent SSF code is probably the easiest way forward.
I will probably get to this in the next couple of months.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Overlap in amt package with ctmm home ranges
messages.subject_clean: Overlap in amt package with ctmm home ranges
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

ctmm::overlap() does not estimate the 95% geometric overlap in coverage areas. That argument is for the confidence intervals. Geometric overlap measures are sensitive to the choice of coverage probability and do not account for non-uniform space use. By default, ctmm::overlap() calculates a debiased Bhattacharya coefficient: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.13027
and there is an option related to the UDOI, but with a corrected normalization.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: differences between the weighted and non weighted models
messages.subject_clean: differences between the weighted and non weighted models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tobi,

If the sampling is irregular in a kind of uniformly random way, but the effective sample size is very large, then the improvement to AKDE can be very minimal. On the other hand, if you had switched between 5-second sampling and 12-hour sampling at one month into the data collection, or if you had a shorter tracking duration compared to the animal's home-range crossing timescale, then the weights would still be impactful.

https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/eap.1704

We haven't yet examined the impact on RSF estimation, for cases such as yours.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: ctmm.fit vs ctmm.select for mean UDs
messages.subject_clean: ctmm.fit vs ctmm.select for mean UDs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Connie,

You are running ctmm.fit() with no guess object, which just returns an IID model fit, which has the maximum DOF equal to the nominal sample size. This produces a tighter distribution, but is incorrect for non-independent data.

On the other hand, when you run ctmm.select(), some of your DOFs are very small because individuals are not very resident. The estimate is appropriately larger than the data, with correspondingly large confidence intervals. This is a data quality issue, as you are effectively estimating something akin to a dispersal kernel for the population.

Your individual DOFs are: 1.4, 1.8, 2.1, 2.6, 6.7, 13.4. So the first 4 will have negatively biased range estimates without ctmm.boot() and are potentially non-resident.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Stochastic process models of animal movement, maximum entropy, and approximation theory
messages.subject_clean: Stochastic process models of animal movement, maximum entropy, and approximation theory
messages.body_plain:
If anyone is interested in a more mathematical talk on the basic continuous-time stochastic process models used in describing animal movement, which I delivered at the Isaac Newton Institute in Cambridge:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pjmQLkxQpgQ

I detail a class of maximum-entropy stochastic-process models that contains within it all of the continuous-time stationary processes that have been commonly used to model animal movement—including Brownian motion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck motion, and integrated Ornstein-Uhlenbeck motion. Then I show how linear combinations of these maximum-entropy processes can approximate more general stationary processes by way of Padé approximants. I end with discussion of some simpler ways that these stationary processes can be generalized into more realistic non-stationary processes.

messages.subject: Re: TWS 2023 Conference
messages.subject_clean: TWS 2023 Conference
messages.body_plain:
Also at this year's TWS annual conference, I will be delivering a talk on the population distribution estimation method now in ctmm (details below):

Presentation Title: Population range estimation with animal tracking data

Session: Spatial Ecology and Modeling II

Session type: Contributed Oral

Presentation Time: Wednesday, November 08, 2023 from 4:00 PM - 4:15 PM

Room: Laffoon (East Tower, 1st Floor Lobby Level)

Estimating the spatial range of herds, colonies, and populations is a common applied problem, yet conventional approaches to this task have lacked the capability to satisfy the basic assumptions of tracking data or provide reliable uncertainty estimates. Traditional methods have largely centered on either combining individually estimated home-range areas into a union or combining individual-level tracking data within a single distribution estimator. In part, because of the strong biases associated with these approaches, considerable attention has been focused on the required number tracked individuals to make population-level inferences. In this talk, I introduce a population kernel density estimator (PKDE), wherein the bandwidth is optimized targeting a hierarchical population model, while simultaneously accounting for temporal autocorrelation in the individual-level data. An uncertainty estimate is also provided. Using empirical data on grizzly bears (Ursus arctos horribilis), I show that required number of tracked individuals to obtain relatively unbiased PKDE estimates is few.

2) I do need to ponder my non-resident movement models a bit more, so thank you for looking at my sample dataset. In most of my datasets (with small sample sizes), I have been able to identify the "dispersal/migration" portion of the track and am interested in summarizing these movements as their "dispersal range." I realize this might not be ideal, so it would be great to hear your insights on this, given new packages (dispfit? or others?) or if we can present all results using ctmm with some limits/major caveats.

Would an IID model fit with caveats be ok to consider or better to have overestimated UDs using the ctmm.select function? I am asking about the mathematical point of view as I am aware that it may also be dependent on the scientific question/objectives.

Connie

messages.subject: Re: ctmm.fit vs ctmm.select for mean UDs
messages.subject_clean: ctmm.fit vs ctmm.select for mean UDs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Connie,
ctmm.fit() will fit and keep all of the specified parameters. ctmm.select() will drop the unsupported parameters. In almost all use cases, you want to use the latter.
The documentation is using ctmm.fit() in specific cases where I know that is safe to do (for computational speed), but also informing you not to do that on your data (unless you know better).
If you are able to segment your data into resident segments and dispersal segments, then I would recommend estimating separate ranges for each, and reporting them separately. Also IIRC, I believe you were using mean() when you probably want to be using pkde(), but the latter is more sensitive to data quality issues. The former is the mean of the sample, while the latter is the extrapolated population range.
When you have a small effective sample size (unless its from location error) then the AKDE is underestimated, but you still get appropriately wide confidence intervals. Switching to IID KDE is exacerbating that negative bias.
Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Continuous-time encounter measures and their estimation
messages.subject_clean: Continuous-time encounter measures and their estimation
messages.body_plain:
If anyone is interested in a talk on continuous-time measures of interactions and encounters, which I delivered at the Isaac Newton Institute in Cambridge:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cPPfvfu_xEk

Animal tracking data comprise locations sampled at discrete times, which may only provide a sparse representation of the true movement path, and where the sampled times may not be synchronous across individuals. Therefore, measures that test for encounters only at sampled times can miss encounters that occur during the observation period, and will yield differentially biased encounter-rate estimates, with more underestimation at coarser sampling rates and for more tortuous movement processes. In this talk, I discuss measures based on continuous-time stochastic process models that avoid these biases and provide uncertainty estimates that reflect imperfect observation.

Thank you in advance,
Soham Mehta

messages.body_plain:
Hi Soham,

In the cases where there is a clear separation between the selected model's theoretical semi-variance and the data's empirical variogram, outside of the CIs, I would definitely look to segment the data.

As for estimating 2nd-order selection versus 3rd-order selection, with the present kinds of RSF models, I think you need to do that in two stages or at two levels, with the home-range centers and foray locations sampled from a separate process. I think, data-wise, that's probably going to be very hard to do without multiple individuals, but I'm working on some functional response code at the moment when using mean() on multiple RSFs.

Best,
Chris

> > > Hi Soham,
> > >
> > > In the cases where there is a clear separation between the selected model's theoretical semi-variance and the data's empirical variogram, outside of the CIs, I would definitely look to segment the data.
> > >
> > > As for estimating 2nd-order selection versus 3rd-order selection, with the present kinds of RSF models, I think you need to do that in two stages or at two levels, with the home-range centers and foray locations sampled from a separate process. I think, data-wise, that's probably going to be very hard to do without multiple individuals, but I'm working on some functional response code at the moment when using mean() on multiple RSFs.
> > >
> > > Best,
> > > Chris

> > > >
> > > > I have been seeing other people's doubts about meeting the range residency assumption. However, I wanted to confirm somethings about some of my variograms.
> > > >
> > > > 1. If an asymptote is observed and then the line is trending upwards towards the very end would I need to trunicate the data further. I ask this because (a) some of the dogs already have only a few days of data (e.g. 20-40 days),(b) I have already subsetted the data into seasons (summer, winter, monsoon) to showcase different distributions (c) we know that free-ranging dogs do not really 'migrate' but may frequently foray and may visit specific sites repeatedly where they might be a food source. So if I were to remove those locations it would affect my habitat selection (2nd order) analysis. So in the case of dogs with low sampling time and an increasing trend in the end, should I just use those estimates and report the trend observed? What would you recommend?
> > > >
> > > > 2. Some of them tend to have a decreasing trend in the second half of the empirical variogram. What do you advise I do about those?
> > > >
> > > > 3. I used the ctmm.guess & ctmm.select fucntions to fit the movement model. However, the movement model fit seemed a little weird for a select few which I have posted. How can I change that so it is more accurate?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Thank you in advance,
> > > > Soham Mehta
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday, March 31, 2022 at 9:26:17 AM UTC-4 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > Hi Yu Lei,
> > > > >
> > > > > Seeing this large of a discrepancy between the empirical and theoretical (fitted) variograms suggests that there is some non-stationary behavior in the data that needs to be taken into account. I would look to see if the data needs to be segmented at some time(s) because of a range shift or dispersal event of some kind.
> > > > >
> > > > > The tau parameters are as you have noted. The diffusion rate parameter is new and will be described in an upcoming paper. I introduced this for people to be able to quantify a rate of movement in data that are too coarse for speed estimation, but not so coarse that they are IID.
> > > > >
> > > > > Best,
> > > > > Chris
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wednesday, March 30, 2022 at 9:21:48 PM UTC-4 leial...@126.com wrote:
> > > > > > Hi Chris,
> > > > > > Thanks for your prompt reply.  I have another two questions here.
> > > > > > First, i find the GUESS i manually fitted (red line in below ) is different with the fitted GUESS of best model via ctmm.select (green line). Should i according to the fitted model result to estimate home range or adjusting the model GUESS until close i wished. If necessary to adjust, how to realize?
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The second question is about movement parameters from ctmm.select function (see below).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Two parameter (home range crossing time (τp )and directional persistence timescale (τv )) were referred in this paper  Medici <https://movementecologyjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s40462-022-00313-w#auth-E__P_-Medici> 2022 (https://doi.org/10.1186/s40462-022-00313-w),  does it mean τ position and τ velocity separately ?
> > > > > > And i confuesd on diffusion parameter which have rare interpretation before, it means movement or dispersal range per day ? if so , can i use it to quantify the movement or space use of animal individual during study period?
> > > > > > Thanks for any suggestions.
> > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > Yu Lei
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 在2022年3月28日星期一 UTC+8 12:30:03<chris.h...@gmail.com> 写道：

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > The ideal variogram of a range resident individual is one that has a flat asymptote, like F04 & M03 in the figure. However, I think that these variograms are all fully zoomed out, and the last half of a variogram is pretty erroneous, so variograms like F01 & F15 are okay too.

> > > > > > > The middling variograms, like F03 and F06 are somewhat questionable, and I would look at whether their area estimates and DOFs fall within the spread of the population.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > We have a number of features to help with this identification, including the CI="Gauss" argument to variogram() and the cluster() function, and we are testing some cross validation methods as well.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > > Chris
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Friday, March 25, 2022 at 8:49:07 AM UTC-4 yu lei wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hi Chris
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >  Thanks so much for your reply last time.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >  I know the AKDE is suited for  range residents, and we can determine whether an individual exhibit range residency via visual SVF with reaching asymptotes  or the DOF area value.
> > > > > > > >        However, I'm not sure when the variogram asympetote can indicate residency.  Recently,  i saw a figure (posted below ) in the preprint paper (https://osf.io/ka5t6) , it seems stable variograms have kinds of shapes, including bell, hump shapes, even some consistent upward lines which should not be stable events i think.
> > > > > > > >        I only suppose that when the vairogram have a flatten asymptote (like a straight line) can represents range residency before,  After saw the figure, i was confused about this question.
> > > > > > > >  Thanks for any suggestions.
> > > > > > > >  Best,
> > > > > > > > Yu Lei
> > > > > > > >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Soham,

I wouldn't worry about the very end of the variogram, as that part lacks confidence. I would worry about the asymptotes not matching up like the last 4. That usually means that the process changed and the variance of multiple behaviors is larger than the variance of the individual behaviors.

You can't identify absolute times from the variogram (only lengths of time or time lag). For segmenting like that, I would recommend clustering algorithms like kmeans, kmedians, and segclust2d.

Best,
Chris

Best

Bummer!! Glad I didn't waste more time trying to finagle it then :D

Follow up question for when I rerun these models then! This is how I fit the AKDEs yesterday:

MantiWinter.telem <- ctmm::as.telemetry(MantiWinter,  drop = FALSE)

man.win.guess <- lapply(MantiWinter.telem, FUN = ctmm.guess, interactive = FALSE)
length(m.man.win.guess)  ## 31 season-years in manti winter
M.OUF_Lst_Mantiwin <- list()
AKDE_Lst_Mantiwin <- list()
# fit ctmm model for each guy
for(i in 1:length(MantiWinter.telem)){
  M.OUF_Lst_Mantiwin[[i]] <- ctmm.select(MantiWinter.telem[[i]], m.man.win.guess[[i]])
  AKDE_Lst_Mantiwin[[i]] <- akde(MantiWinter.telem[[i]],M.OUF_Lst_Mantiwin[[i]] )  ## akde
}

saveRDS(AKDE_Lst_Mantiwin, "SeasonalAKDE/AKDE_Manti_winter.rds")

I  created these datasets clumped by site because there are far enough apart that I created all my spatial rasters separately (for a different analysis). If I combine these all  and rerun the AKDE, should that save the problem? My sites are pretty spread out in Utah so I didn't think fitting them all to the same grid would be efficient.

Thanks again!!

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Chris, this is great info!
I reran my code for different datasets and the pkde() seems to be working and the UDS look more reasonable, so that is good news! However, I ran into an error message on a couple of datasets using the same code after running pkde(): "Error in rep(0, gridsize - 1) : invalid 'times' argument." My input data are in the same format for ones that look like they run successfully and ones that throw the error.
The error also occurs for the example dataset I shared earlier on dropbox. I amended the code at the end to show the steps, though it is just using PKDE <- pkde(data_tel, UDS) instead of the mean(UDS) at the last line.
I'm interested in learning more about the pkde(), so if there are any materials that is available for others that are unable to attend your upcoming talk at TWS or other related references, please let me know.
Thanks again for your quick response!
Best,
Connie

On Thursday, September 21, 2023 at 5:04:15 PM UTC-4 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Connie,
> ctmm.fit() will fit and keep all of the specified parameters. ctmm.select() will drop the unsupported parameters. In almost all use cases, you want to use the latter.
> The documentation is using ctmm.fit() in specific cases where I know that is safe to do (for computational speed), but also informing you not to do that on your data (unless you know better).
> If you are able to segment your data into resident segments and dispersal segments, then I would recommend estimating separate ranges for each, and reporting them separately. Also IIRC, I believe you were using mean() when you probably want to be using pkde(), but the latter is more sensitive to data quality issues. The former is the mean of the sample, while the latter is the extrapolated population range.
> When you have a small effective sample size (unless its from location error) then the AKDE is underestimated, but you still get appropriately wide confidence intervals. Switching to IID KDE is exacerbating that negative bias.
> Best,
> Chris
>
>
> On Thursday, September 21, 2023 at 3:59:53 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > Hi Chris,
> > Thank you for this explanation - there is a lot here to unpack and appreciate your time and expertise!
> > 1) I was mainly surprised that it would run without a guess object, so this clarifies what is happening - thanks! I was also able to run the ctmm.fit with a guess object (ran ctmm.guess first) and results were similar to ctmm.select (with guess object), but not exact (amended my R code in dropbox if you wanted to take a look). Can you please explain this? For estimating aKDEs for populations (n > 1), I understand that the best method would be to run ctmm.select() with the guess object (after running ctmm.guess), such as the example you have presented in the past webinar. But I was confused by the documentation, where it uses ctmm.fit with guess and says "in general, you want to run ctmm.select instead" (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/ctmm.fit.html).
> > 2) I do need to ponder my non-resident movement models a bit more, so thank you for looking at my sample dataset. In most of my datasets (with small sample sizes), I have been able to identify the "dispersal/migration" portion of the track and am interested in summarizing these movements as their "dispersal range." I have been exploring aKDEs for resident and dispersing behaviors to keep the method consistent within a dataset and balance timelines. I realize this might not be ideal, so it would be great to hear your insights on this, given new packages (dispfit? or others?) or if we can present all results using ctmm with some limits/major caveats.
> > 3) Thanks for the tip about ctmm.boot - this was my next step, given time. However, this might not be appropriate for datasets with only n = 1 (or if we run out of time), so I'm wondering how to best handle aKDEs for one individual or small sample sizes without bootstrapping. Would an IID model fit with caveats be ok to consider or better to have overestimated UDs using the ctmm.select function? I am asking about the mathematical point of view as I am aware that it may also be dependent on the scientific question/objectives.
> > Best,
> > Connie
> >
> > On Sunday, September 17, 2023 at 9:41:19 PM UTC-4 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > Hi Connie,
> > >
> > > You are running ctmm.fit() with no guess object, which just returns an IID model fit, which has the maximum DOF equal to the nominal sample size. This produces a tighter distribution, but is incorrect for non-independent data.
> > >
> > > On the other hand, when you run ctmm.select(), some of your DOFs are very small because individuals are not very resident. The estimate is appropriately larger than the data, with correspondingly large confidence intervals. This is a data quality issue, as you are effectively estimating something akin to a dispersal kernel for the population.
> > >
> > > Your individual DOFs are: 1.4, 1.8, 2.1, 2.6, 6.7, 13.4. So the first 4 will have negatively biased range estimates without ctmm.boot() and are potentially non-resident.
> > >
> > > Best,
> > > Chris
> > >
> > > On Thursday, September 14, 2023 at 7:55:31 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > > > Hello!
> > > > I have been using the code given during the spring webinar to create mean UDs (very helpful - thanks!) but noticed that they produce really large areas that seem to be overestimations. This is using the ctmm.select function after running ctmm.guess an averaging the UDs of individuals within a population. When I used ctmm.fit (also provided as an example method, but ran for individual akdes), and averaged the resulting UDs, the results seemed more reasonable for home ranges. I tried to read more about how these differ, but I am not understanding why/when one is preferred. I do think I have relatively small sample sizes, but the ctmm.fit seems to be doing what we need.
> > > > The edited R code and same sample data files are in the same dropbox location.
> > > > Thank you!
> > > > Connie

Running everything at once will not put them on the same grid, but on grids of the same resolution and alignment (extents can differ). This will work fine unless you have tiny and large home ranges in the same study, where the tiny resolutions applied to the largest home ranges will eat all of your RAM. I have to add some code to be able to handle that in an automated way.

You can reuse the fits,  M.OUF_Lst_Mantiwin, as long as they were calculated in the same projection.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,
I should note that this error message started showing up when running more than one dataset, but after I restarted R a few times, it seemed to have resolved so maybe it was just a glitch? However, I now get another error message and I am not sure if it is related, so I have included it in this same thread. After running pkde() for two individuals, I got a warning message first: "Warning message: In akde(data, CTMM = UD, kernel = kernel, weights = weights, ref = ref,  :  Population fit object returned. DOF[area] = 1.79492098138809e-07" and then I get error messages when trying to plot it or trying to export it as a shapefile to explore further. When I plotted the individual aKDEs, I was able to see them as overlapping. I placed the dataset that was giving me the error in dropbox and the new code is at the end. Any insights would be much appreciated!
Best,
Connie

On Saturday, September 23, 2023 at 12:20:38 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> Thanks, Chris, this is great info!
> I reran my code for different datasets and the pkde() seems to be working and the UDS look more reasonable, so that is good news! However, I ran into an error message on a couple of datasets using the same code after running pkde(): "Error in rep(0, gridsize - 1) : invalid 'times' argument." My input data are in the same format for ones that look like they run successfully and ones that throw the error.
> The error also occurs for the example dataset I shared earlier on dropbox. I amended the code at the end to show the steps, though it is just using PKDE <- pkde(data_tel, UDS) instead of the mean(UDS) at the last line.
> I'm interested in learning more about the pkde(), so if there are any materials that is available for others that are unable to attend your upcoming talk at TWS or other related references, please let me know.
> Thanks again for your quick response!
> Best,
> Connie
> On Thursday, September 21, 2023 at 5:04:15 PM UTC-4 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hi Connie,
> > ctmm.fit() will fit and keep all of the specified parameters. ctmm.select() will drop the unsupported parameters. In almost all use cases, you want to use the latter.
> > The documentation is using ctmm.fit() in specific cases where I know that is safe to do (for computational speed), but also informing you not to do that on your data (unless you know better).
> > If you are able to segment your data into resident segments and dispersal segments, then I would recommend estimating separate ranges for each, and reporting them separately. Also IIRC, I believe you were using mean() when you probably want to be using pkde(), but the latter is more sensitive to data quality issues. The former is the mean of the sample, while the latter is the extrapolated population range.
> > When you have a small effective sample size (unless its from location error) then the AKDE is underestimated, but you still get appropriately wide confidence intervals. Switching to IID KDE is exacerbating that negative bias.
> > Best,
> > Chris
> >
> >
> > On Thursday, September 21, 2023 at 3:59:53 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > > Hi Chris,
> > > Thank you for this explanation - there is a lot here to unpack and appreciate your time and expertise!
> > > 1) I was mainly surprised that it would run without a guess object, so this clarifies what is happening - thanks! I was also able to run the ctmm.fit with a guess object (ran ctmm.guess first) and results were similar to ctmm.select (with guess object), but not exact (amended my R code in dropbox if you wanted to take a look). Can you please explain this? For estimating aKDEs for populations (n > 1), I understand that the best method would be to run ctmm.select() with the guess object (after running ctmm.guess), such as the example you have presented in the past webinar. But I was confused by the documentation, where it uses ctmm.fit with guess and says "in general, you want to run ctmm.select instead" (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/ctmm.fit.html).
> > > 2) I do need to ponder my non-resident movement models a bit more, so thank you for looking at my sample dataset. In most of my datasets (with small sample sizes), I have been able to identify the "dispersal/migration" portion of the track and am interested in summarizing these movements as their "dispersal range." I have been exploring aKDEs for resident and dispersing behaviors to keep the method consistent within a dataset and balance timelines. I realize this might not be ideal, so it would be great to hear your insights on this, given new packages (dispfit? or others?) or if we can present all results using ctmm with some limits/major caveats.
> > > 3) Thanks for the tip about ctmm.boot - this was my next step, given time. However, this might not be appropriate for datasets with only n = 1 (or if we run out of time), so I'm wondering how to best handle aKDEs for one individual or small sample sizes without bootstrapping. Would an IID model fit with caveats be ok to consider or better to have overestimated UDs using the ctmm.select function? I am asking about the mathematical point of view as I am aware that it may also be dependent on the scientific question/objectives.
> > > Best,
> > > Connie
> > >
> > > On Sunday, September 17, 2023 at 9:41:19 PM UTC-4 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Hi Connie,
> > > >
> > > > You are running ctmm.fit() with no guess object, which just returns an IID model fit, which has the maximum DOF equal to the nominal sample size. This produces a tighter distribution, but is incorrect for non-independent data.
> > > >
> > > > On the other hand, when you run ctmm.select(), some of your DOFs are very small because individuals are not very resident. The estimate is appropriately larger than the data, with correspondingly large confidence intervals. This is a data quality issue, as you are effectively estimating something akin to a dispersal kernel for the population.
> > > >
> > > > Your individual DOFs are: 1.4, 1.8, 2.1, 2.6, 6.7, 13.4. So the first 4 will have negatively biased range estimates without ctmm.boot() and are potentially non-resident.
> > > >
> > > > Best,
> > > > Chris
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday, September 14, 2023 at 7:55:31 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > > > > Hello!
> > > > > I have been using the code given during the spring webinar to create mean UDs (very helpful - thanks!) but noticed that they produce really large areas that seem to be overestimations. This is using the ctmm.select function after running ctmm.guess an averaging the UDs of individuals within a population. When I used ctmm.fit (also provided as an example method, but ran for individual akdes), and averaged the resulting UDs, the results seemed more reasonable for home ranges. I tried to read more about how these differ, but I am not understanding why/when one is preferred. I do think I have relatively small sample sizes, but the ctmm.fit seems to be doing what we need.
> > > > > The edited R code and same sample data files are in the same dropbox location.
> > > > > Thank you!
> > > > > Connie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Connie,

Population fit object returned. DOF[area] = 1.79492098138809e-07

This is a problematic warning message. This effective sample size is almost zero. The CIs will be so wide, you can't really export this or do anything with it.

I don't think its safe to run pkde() on just two individuals. That would be like running akde() on two locations. I can work on coding that to be more robust, but I would never trust that output.

Best,
Chris

On Sunday, September 24, 2023 at 8:36:57 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> Hi Chris,
> I should note that this error message started showing up when running more than one dataset, but after I restarted R a few times, it seemed to have resolved so maybe it was just a glitch? However, I now get another error message and I am not sure if it is related, so I have included it in this same thread. After running pkde() for two individuals, I got a warning message first: "Warning message: In akde(data, CTMM = UD, kernel = kernel, weights = weights, ref = ref,  :  Population fit object returned. DOF[area] = 1.79492098138809e-07" and then I get error messages when trying to plot it or trying to export it as a shapefile to explore further. When I plotted the individual aKDEs, I was able to see them as overlapping. I placed the dataset that was giving me the error in dropbox and the new code is at the end. Any insights would be much appreciated!
> Best,
> Connie
>
> On Saturday, September 23, 2023 at 12:20:38 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > Thanks, Chris, this is great info!
> > I reran my code for different datasets and the pkde() seems to be working and the UDS look more reasonable, so that is good news! However, I ran into an error message on a couple of datasets using the same code after running pkde(): "Error in rep(0, gridsize - 1) : invalid 'times' argument." My input data are in the same format for ones that look like they run successfully and ones that throw the error.
> > The error also occurs for the example dataset I shared earlier on dropbox. I amended the code at the end to show the steps, though it is just using PKDE <- pkde(data_tel, UDS) instead of the mean(UDS) at the last line.
> > I'm interested in learning more about the pkde(), so if there are any materials that is available for others that are unable to attend your upcoming talk at TWS or other related references, please let me know.
> > Thanks again for your quick response!
> > Best,
> > Connie
> > On Thursday, September 21, 2023 at 5:04:15 PM UTC-4 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > Hi Connie,
> > > ctmm.fit() will fit and keep all of the specified parameters. ctmm.select() will drop the unsupported parameters. In almost all use cases, you want to use the latter.
> > > The documentation is using ctmm.fit() in specific cases where I know that is safe to do (for computational speed), but also informing you not to do that on your data (unless you know better).
> > > If you are able to segment your data into resident segments and dispersal segments, then I would recommend estimating separate ranges for each, and reporting them separately. Also IIRC, I believe you were using mean() when you probably want to be using pkde(), but the latter is more sensitive to data quality issues. The former is the mean of the sample, while the latter is the extrapolated population range.
> > > When you have a small effective sample size (unless its from location error) then the AKDE is underestimated, but you still get appropriately wide confidence intervals. Switching to IID KDE is exacerbating that negative bias.
> > > Best,
> > > Chris
> > >
> > >
> > > On Thursday, September 21, 2023 at 3:59:53 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > > > Hi Chris,
> > > > Thank you for this explanation - there is a lot here to unpack and appreciate your time and expertise!
> > > > 1) I was mainly surprised that it would run without a guess object, so this clarifies what is happening - thanks! I was also able to run the ctmm.fit with a guess object (ran ctmm.guess first) and results were similar to ctmm.select (with guess object), but not exact (amended my R code in dropbox if you wanted to take a look). Can you please explain this? For estimating aKDEs for populations (n > 1), I understand that the best method would be to run ctmm.select() with the guess object (after running ctmm.guess), such as the example you have presented in the past webinar. But I was confused by the documentation, where it uses ctmm.fit with guess and says "in general, you want to run ctmm.select instead" (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/ctmm.fit.html).
> > > > 2) I do need to ponder my non-resident movement models a bit more, so thank you for looking at my sample dataset. In most of my datasets (with small sample sizes), I have been able to identify the "dispersal/migration" portion of the track and am interested in summarizing these movements as their "dispersal range." I have been exploring aKDEs for resident and dispersing behaviors to keep the method consistent within a dataset and balance timelines. I realize this might not be ideal, so it would be great to hear your insights on this, given new packages (dispfit? or others?) or if we can present all results using ctmm with some limits/major caveats.
> > > > 3) Thanks for the tip about ctmm.boot - this was my next step, given time. However, this might not be appropriate for datasets with only n = 1 (or if we run out of time), so I'm wondering how to best handle aKDEs for one individual or small sample sizes without bootstrapping. Would an IID model fit with caveats be ok to consider or better to have overestimated UDs using the ctmm.select function? I am asking about the mathematical point of view as I am aware that it may also be dependent on the scientific question/objectives.
> > > > Best,
> > > > Connie
> > > >
> > > > On Sunday, September 17, 2023 at 9:41:19 PM UTC-4 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > Hi Connie,
> > > > >
> > > > > You are running ctmm.fit() with no guess object, which just returns an IID model fit, which has the maximum DOF equal to the nominal sample size. This produces a tighter distribution, but is incorrect for non-independent data.
> > > > >
> > > > > On the other hand, when you run ctmm.select(), some of your DOFs are very small because individuals are not very resident. The estimate is appropriately larger than the data, with correspondingly large confidence intervals. This is a data quality issue, as you are effectively estimating something akin to a dispersal kernel for the population.
> > > > >
> > > > > Your individual DOFs are: 1.4, 1.8, 2.1, 2.6, 6.7, 13.4. So the first 4 will have negatively biased range estimates without ctmm.boot() and are potentially non-resident.
> > > > >
> > > > > Best,
> > > > > Chris
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thursday, September 14, 2023 at 7:55:31 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > > > > > Hello!
> > > > > > I have been using the code given during the spring webinar to create mean UDs (very helpful - thanks!) but noticed that they produce really large areas that seem to be overestimations. This is using the ctmm.select function after running ctmm.guess an averaging the UDs of individuals within a population. When I used ctmm.fit (also provided as an example method, but ran for individual akdes), and averaged the resulting UDs, the results seemed more reasonable for home ranges. I tried to read more about how these differ, but I am not understanding why/when one is preferred. I do think I have relatively small sample sizes, but the ctmm.fit seems to be doing what we need.
> > > > > > The edited R code and same sample data files are in the same dropbox location.
> > > > > > Thank you!
> > > > > > Connie

messages.subject: Re: ctmm.fit vs ctmm.select for mean UDs
messages.subject_clean: ctmm.fit vs ctmm.select for mean UDs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,
Thanks for looking into this! The main objective for summarizing our data, with a small sample size, is to have a better way to represent area-use, though it is obviously going to be limited statistically. In the past, we have resorted to calculating the mean KDE with the knowledge that this is not ideal. After looking at the results from the pkde() function, it seemed like the resulting UDs were in between UDs using the IID model fit and UDs calculated as the mean UDs (aKDEs). So, do you suggest that for certain sample sizes (some small threshold?), that it would be better not to use pkde() and use the mean UD (or other method)?
Thank you!
Connie

On Monday, September 25, 2023 at 7:20:42 PM UTC-4 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Connie,
>
> Population fit object returned. DOF[area] = 1.79492098138809e-07
>
> This is a problematic warning message. This effective sample size is almost zero. The CIs will be so wide, you can't really export this or do anything with it.
>
> I don't think its safe to run pkde() on just two individuals. That would be like running akde() on two locations. I can work on coding that to be more robust, but I would never trust that output.
>
> Best,
> Chris
>
> On Sunday, September 24, 2023 at 8:36:57 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > Hi Chris,
> > I should note that this error message started showing up when running more than one dataset, but after I restarted R a few times, it seemed to have resolved so maybe it was just a glitch? However, I now get another error message and I am not sure if it is related, so I have included it in this same thread. After running pkde() for two individuals, I got a warning message first: "Warning message: In akde(data, CTMM = UD, kernel = kernel, weights = weights, ref = ref,  :  Population fit object returned. DOF[area] = 1.79492098138809e-07" and then I get error messages when trying to plot it or trying to export it as a shapefile to explore further. When I plotted the individual aKDEs, I was able to see them as overlapping. I placed the dataset that was giving me the error in dropbox and the new code is at the end. Any insights would be much appreciated!
> > Best,
> > Connie
> >
> > On Saturday, September 23, 2023 at 12:20:38 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > > Thanks, Chris, this is great info!
> > > I reran my code for different datasets and the pkde() seems to be working and the UDS look more reasonable, so that is good news! However, I ran into an error message on a couple of datasets using the same code after running pkde(): "Error in rep(0, gridsize - 1) : invalid 'times' argument." My input data are in the same format for ones that look like they run successfully and ones that throw the error.
> > > The error also occurs for the example dataset I shared earlier on dropbox. I amended the code at the end to show the steps, though it is just using PKDE <- pkde(data_tel, UDS) instead of the mean(UDS) at the last line.
> > > I'm interested in learning more about the pkde(), so if there are any materials that is available for others that are unable to attend your upcoming talk at TWS or other related references, please let me know.
> > > Thanks again for your quick response!
> > > Best,
> > > Connie
> > > On Thursday, September 21, 2023 at 5:04:15 PM UTC-4 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Hi Connie,
> > > > ctmm.fit() will fit and keep all of the specified parameters. ctmm.select() will drop the unsupported parameters. In almost all use cases, you want to use the latter.
> > > > The documentation is using ctmm.fit() in specific cases where I know that is safe to do (for computational speed), but also informing you not to do that on your data (unless you know better).
> > > > If you are able to segment your data into resident segments and dispersal segments, then I would recommend estimating separate ranges for each, and reporting them separately. Also IIRC, I believe you were using mean() when you probably want to be using pkde(), but the latter is more sensitive to data quality issues. The former is the mean of the sample, while the latter is the extrapolated population range.
> > > > When you have a small effective sample size (unless its from location error) then the AKDE is underestimated, but you still get appropriately wide confidence intervals. Switching to IID KDE is exacerbating that negative bias.
> > > > Best,
> > > > Chris
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday, September 21, 2023 at 3:59:53 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > > > > Hi Chris,
> > > > > Thank you for this explanation - there is a lot here to unpack and appreciate your time and expertise!
> > > > > 1) I was mainly surprised that it would run without a guess object, so this clarifies what is happening - thanks! I was also able to run the ctmm.fit with a guess object (ran ctmm.guess first) and results were similar to ctmm.select (with guess object), but not exact (amended my R code in dropbox if you wanted to take a look). Can you please explain this? For estimating aKDEs for populations (n > 1), I understand that the best method would be to run ctmm.select() with the guess object (after running ctmm.guess), such as the example you have presented in the past webinar. But I was confused by the documentation, where it uses ctmm.fit with guess and says "in general, you want to run ctmm.select instead" (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/ctmm.fit.html).
> > > > > 2) I do need to ponder my non-resident movement models a bit more, so thank you for looking at my sample dataset. In most of my datasets (with small sample sizes), I have been able to identify the "dispersal/migration" portion of the track and am interested in summarizing these movements as their "dispersal range." I have been exploring aKDEs for resident and dispersing behaviors to keep the method consistent within a dataset and balance timelines. I realize this might not be ideal, so it would be great to hear your insights on this, given new packages (dispfit? or others?) or if we can present all results using ctmm with some limits/major caveats.
> > > > > 3) Thanks for the tip about ctmm.boot - this was my next step, given time. However, this might not be appropriate for datasets with only n = 1 (or if we run out of time), so I'm wondering how to best handle aKDEs for one individual or small sample sizes without bootstrapping. Would an IID model fit with caveats be ok to consider or better to have overestimated UDs using the ctmm.select function? I am asking about the mathematical point of view as I am aware that it may also be dependent on the scientific question/objectives.
> > > > > Best,
> > > > > Connie
> > > > >
> > > > > On Sunday, September 17, 2023 at 9:41:19 PM UTC-4 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > Hi Connie,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > You are running ctmm.fit() with no guess object, which just returns an IID model fit, which has the maximum DOF equal to the nominal sample size. This produces a tighter distribution, but is incorrect for non-independent data.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On the other hand, when you run ctmm.select(), some of your DOFs are very small because individuals are not very resident. The estimate is appropriately larger than the data, with correspondingly large confidence intervals. This is a data quality issue, as you are effectively estimating something akin to a dispersal kernel for the population.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Your individual DOFs are: 1.4, 1.8, 2.1, 2.6, 6.7, 13.4. So the first 4 will have negatively biased range estimates without ctmm.boot() and are potentially non-resident.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > Chris
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Thursday, September 14, 2023 at 7:55:31 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > > > > > > Hello!
> > > > > > > I have been using the code given during the spring webinar to create mean UDs (very helpful - thanks!) but noticed that they produce really large areas that seem to be overestimations. This is using the ctmm.select function after running ctmm.guess an averaging the UDs of individuals within a population. When I used ctmm.fit (also provided as an example method, but ran for individual akdes), and averaged the resulting UDs, the results seemed more reasonable for home ranges. I tried to read more about how these differ, but I am not understanding why/when one is preferred. I do think I have relatively small sample sizes, but the ctmm.fit seems to be doing what we need.
> > > > > > > The edited R code and same sample data files are in the same dropbox location.
> > > > > > > Thank you!
> > > > > > > Connie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kristin,

Yes, those calls to akde() are independent and so the grid resolutions will not come out to be the same unless you force them to be with the grid argument.

You want to call akde(MantiWinter.telem,M.OUF_Lst_Mantiwin) instead.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: ctmm.fit vs ctmm.select for mean UDs
messages.subject_clean: ctmm.fit vs ctmm.select for mean UDs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Connie,

Thanks for the example data. I noticed that some numerical gradient code wasn't doing a good job in that example and upgraded that code to analytic formulas, which I tested to work much better. This update is on Github now, however:

The PKDE estimate does not come out to be good with these two individuals because you get variance collapse in the population model estimates, in that the uncertainty in the individual parameter estimates is large enough to explain all of the variation in the data.

In situations like this, assuming that you have to report something, I would run pkde() and mean() on the UDs and then take the larger of the two estimates. mean() does not extrapolate from the sample to the population like pkde() does, but with really weak data (like only 2 points here) pkde() can suffer more from variance collapse.

Best,
Chris

After looking at the results from the pkde() function, it seemed like the resulting UDs were in between UDs using the IID model fit and UDs calculated as the mean UDs (aKDEs). > > > > > Hi Connie,
> > > > > ctmm.fit() will fit and keep all of the specified parameters. ctmm.select() will drop the unsupported parameters. In almost all use cases, you want to use the latter.
> > > > > The documentation is using ctmm.fit() in specific cases where I know that is safe to do (for computational speed), but also informing you not to do that on your data (unless you know better).
> > > > > If you are able to segment your data into resident segments and dispersal segments, then I would recommend estimating separate ranges for each, and reporting them separately. Also IIRC, I believe you were using mean() when you probably want to be using pkde(), but the latter is more sensitive to data quality issues. The former is the mean of the sample, while the latter is the extrapolated population range.
> > > > > When you have a small effective sample size (unless its from location error) then the AKDE is underestimated, but you still get appropriately wide confidence intervals. Switching to IID KDE is exacerbating that negative bias.
> > > > > Best,
> > > > > Chris

> > > > > > 1) I was mainly surprised that it would run without a guess object, so this clarifies what is happening - thanks! Can you please explain this? For estimating aKDEs for populations (n > 1), I understand that the best method would be to run ctmm.select() with the guess object (after running ctmm.guess), such as the example you have presented in the past webinar. But I was confused by the documentation, where it uses ctmm.fit with guess and says "in general, you want to run ctmm.select instead" (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/ctmm.fit.html).
> > > > > > 2) I do need to ponder my non-resident movement models a bit more, so thank you for looking at my sample dataset. In most of my datasets (with small sample sizes), I have been able to identify the "dispersal/migration" portion of the track and am interested in summarizing these movements as their "dispersal range." I have been exploring aKDEs for resident and dispersing behaviors to keep the method consistent within a dataset and balance timelines. I realize this might not be ideal, so it would be great to hear your insights on this, given new packages (dispfit? or others?) or if we can present all results using ctmm with some limits/major caveats.
> > > > > > 3) Thanks for the tip about ctmm.boot - this was my next step, given time. However, this might not be appropriate for datasets with only n = 1 (or if we run out of time), so I'm wondering how to best handle aKDEs for one individual or small sample sizes without bootstrapping. Would an IID model fit with caveats be ok to consider or better to have overestimated UDs using the ctmm.select function? I am asking about the mathematical point of view as I am aware that it may also be dependent on the scientific question/objectives.
> > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > Connie
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Sunday, September 17, 2023 at 9:41:19 PM UTC-4 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > > Hi Connie,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > You are running ctmm.fit() with no guess object, which just returns an IID model fit, which has the maximum DOF equal to the nominal sample size. This produces a tighter distribution, but is incorrect for non-independent data.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On the other hand, when you run ctmm.select(), some of your DOFs are very small because individuals are not very resident. The estimate is appropriately larger than the data, with correspondingly large confidence intervals. This is a data quality issue, as you are effectively estimating something akin to a dispersal kernel for the population.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Your individual DOFs are: 1.4, 1.8, 2.1, 2.6, 6.7, 13.4. So the first 4 will have negatively biased range estimates without ctmm.boot() and are potentially non-resident.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > > Chris
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Thursday, September 14, 2023 at 7:55:31 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hello!
> > > > > > > > I have been using the code given during the spring webinar to create mean UDs (very helpful - thanks!) but noticed that they produce really large areas that seem to be overestimations. This is using the ctmm.select function after running ctmm.guess an averaging the UDs of individuals within a population. When I used ctmm.fit (also provided as an example method, but ran for individual akdes), and averaged the resulting UDs, the results seemed more reasonable for home ranges. I tried to read more about how these differ, but I am not understanding why/when one is preferred. I do think I have relatively small sample sizes, but the ctmm.fit seems to be doing what we need.
> > > > > > > > The edited R code and same sample data files are in the same dropbox location.
> > > > > > > > Thank you!
> > > > > > > > Connie

messages.body_plain:
Dear ctmm community,

The Ecological Informatics Lab in the Department of Biology at the University of Central Florida (UCF) in Orlando, Florida, USA is recruiting masters and PhD students to conduct research at the interface of animal movement, statistics, and conservation under the advise of Dr. Christen H. Fleming <https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=NRKu67IAAAAJ>. Potential research topics include: corridor estimation, disease transmission, habitat suitability, and behavioral inference. Students will have the opportunity to advance the open-source "continuous-time movement modeling" (ctmm) R project <https://biology.umd.edu/movement>, work closely with the UCF Marine Turtle Research Group <https://sciences.ucf.edu/biology/marineturtleresearchgroup/>, and collaborate productively with ctmm associated groups at CASUS <https://www.casus.science/research/earth-systems-science/>, UMD <https://science.umd.edu/biology/faganlab/>, UBC <https://noonanm.github.io/QuantitativeEcologyLab/index.html>, and UA <http://www.jmalston.com/research>.

The deadline for applications <https://applynow.graduate.ucf.edu/apply/> is December 1st. A number of fellowships <https://graduate.ucf.edu/fellowships/> are available, and will be met with matching funds. Please contact christen...@ucf.edu before applying—acceptance requires a consenting dissertation advisor.

Best regards,

Christen H. Fleming
